content:
"The flickering blue and red lights of the police cruiser cast dancing shadows on the palm tree, its trunk scarred from the impact. Inside, Senior Constable Miller stifled a sigh. Another night, another DUI. Except this one felt different. The hushed urgency in his partner, Constable Reynolds’s, voice confirmed it. “He’s holding her, Miller. She looks bad.”

Miller approached, the metallic scent of exhaust and spilled liquor thick in the tropical night air. Dale Scott Walkinshaw, a young man whose bewildered eyes held a flicker of fear, cradled the unconscious woman with a tenderness that belied the chaos he’d wrought. Miller knew the routine: secure the scene, assess injuries, breathalyze the driver. Walkinshaw, smelling strongly of alcohol, blew 0.149. Well over the limit.

While paramedics tended to the injured passenger, Walkinshaw was placed in the back of the caged police vehicle. Miller watched him through the rearview, a knot tightening in his stomach. He’d seen the internal report from 2013, the one gathering dust about installing CCTV in these very cages. The one written after another life was lost in police custody. He knew the coroner’s blistering words: “It wasn’t a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when.” Sixteen attempted suicides in three years. Six not discovered until the victim was semi-conscious or worse. These statistics, grim and stark, echoed in his mind.

Walkinshaw slumped against the wire mesh, his head bowed. The sound of the ambulance pulling away for the hospital was the only disturbance in the quiet night. Miller and Reynolds started the engine, preparing for the short drive to the station. Miller glanced in the rearview again. Walkinshaw was still slumped, but his hands were moving, fumbling with something around his neck. A sudden, cold dread washed over Miller. He knew this pattern. He'd trained for this. He'd seen the internal reports, the grim warnings.

“Reynolds,” Miller’s voice was sharper than he intended.

Reynolds, mid-sentence about the noise complaint they were on their way to investigate, looked at him, surprised. “Yeah, Senior Constable?”

“Pull over. Now.” Miller’s heart hammered against his ribs. He instinctively reached for the door handle. The streetlights blurred as Reynolds braked hard, tires squealing. Miller was out of the car before it fully stopped, wrenching open the rear door.

Walkinshaw had fashioned a noose from his shirt, a desperate, clumsy attempt now tightening around his neck. His face was starting to turn an alarming shade of purple. Miller reached in, his fingers fumbling with the knot, the fabric rough against his skin. He swore under his breath, the coroner’s words burning in his ears. This was the 'when.' This was the line in the sand, the consequence of complacency. This was a young man, vulnerable and intoxicated, pushed to the edge in a metal cage without a single camera to watch over him. Miller struggled with the knot, his whole body tense, knowing that in the time it took to drive a few blocks, another life could have been tragically lost, another statistic added to a damning report that nobody seemed to act on."
